ch17.note: The Eurasia Aviation Corporation (欧亚航空), a Sino-German joint airline founded in 1931, was one of Republican China's two main carriers; the other, which Chen also flies, was the Sino-American China National Aviation Corporation (CNAC). These lines ran the perilous wartime routes over the interior.

A set phrase, jie xia qiu (阶下囚), 'the captive below the steps'—one made to kneel at the foot of the dais to await judgment. It carries the sting of a fall from power into a prisoner's helplessness, pointed here because the amiable man described later becomes Chen's own jailer.

ch17.anchor: Inukai Tsuyoshi, once premier of Japan
ch17.note: Inukai Tsuyoshi (犬養毅), prime minister of Japan, was shot dead in office by young naval officers in the May 15 Incident of 1932—a killing that broke party government in prewar Japan and cleared the way for military rule. It is his son, Inukai Ken, who takes part here in the Japanese approaches to Wang Jingwei.

Renders the coarse Chinese curse wangbadan (王八蛋), 'turtle's egg'—roughly 'bastard' or 'son of a bitch.' The turtle carries old associations of cuckoldry and illegitimacy, so the insult is far fouler than its literal English sounds; the text flags it as startlingly out of place.

The Central Training Corps (中央训练团, Zhongyang Xunlian Tuan), the wartime Nationalist organ at Chongqing that put officials and officers through short courses of political indoctrination and retraining, nominally under Chiang Kai-shek himself.

ch17.anchor: the songs of Chu on four sides
ch17.note: The idiom si mian Chu ge (四面楚歌), 'the songs of Chu on every side,' from the last stand of Xiang Yu at Gaixia in 202 BC: hearing the Han armies that ringed him singing the songs of his own Chu homeland, he knew his people had gone over to the enemy—hence to be surrounded, isolated, and doomed.

ch17.anchor: the cry of a crane or the rustle of the wind
ch17.note: The idiom feng sheng he li (风声鹤唳), from the same rout at the Fei River in 383 that gives 'every bush and tree a soldier': the fleeing army was so unnerved it took the cries of cranes and the sound of the wind for pursuing troops—jumpy panic that hears danger in everything.
